title: Repositioning When Your Category Gets Crowded
transcript:
Jordan Vance: Felix, you led positioning at a company that went from being one of five interchangeable tools in a category to being the clear default. What changed?

Felix Nakamura-Odom: We stopped competing on feature checklists. When a category gets crowded, every vendor's homepage starts to look the same, the same three feature icons, the same customer logo wall, the same vague promise of saving time. Buyers can't tell you apart, so they default to price or brand recognition, and you lose both of those fights against bigger competitors. The way out is to find the specific job a specific type of customer is hiring you for that your competitors are structurally worse at serving, and rebuild your entire message around that.

Jordan Vance: How do you find that specific job?

Felix Nakamura-Odom: I look at our best customers, the ones with the highest retention and the most expansion revenue, and I ask what they were doing before us that was so painful they were willing to switch. Not what features they use most, what alternative they were fleeing. In our case, we discovered our best customers weren't switching from a direct competitor at all, they were switching from a combination of spreadsheets and a project tool that wasn't built for their workflow. They weren't buying our category, they were buying relief from a specific, painful, manual process.

Jordan Vance: So how did that change your positioning?

Felix Nakamura-Odom: We stopped calling ourselves a project management tool, which put us in a fight with ten well-funded competitors, and started describing ourselves as the system of record for a specific workflow that only a subset of teams have, client-facing service delivery. That's a smaller total market on paper, but it's a market where we have almost no credible competition, because the generic tools don't model the workflow correctly and the tools built for that workflow are outdated and expensive. Our win rate against anyone in that narrower category went from around thirty percent to over seventy percent within two quarters.

Jordan Vance: Did narrowing the positioning shrink your funnel?

Felix Nakamura-Odom: Total top-of-funnel volume dropped, yes, because we stopped attracting people who were never going to be a good fit anyway. But qualified pipeline and win rate both went up, and so did average deal size, because we were finally speaking directly to the buyer who most needed us instead of trying to be everything to everyone. The volume drop scared the team for about a month until the downstream numbers came in.

Jordan Vance: What's the one thing someone should do if they suspect their positioning has gone generic?

Felix Nakamura-Odom: Read your last twenty lost-deal notes and your last twenty customer testimonials side by side. If the language in your marketing doesn't match the specific words your best customers use to describe why they needed you, you're probably describing your category instead of your differentiation. Rewrite your homepage headline using their words, not your internal feature vocabulary.
